title: Introduction to LLM serving with SGLang - Philip Kiely and Yineng Zhang, Baseten

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is primarily about SGLang as an LLM/VLM serving framework, covering inference performance, CUDA Graph batching, and speculative decoding. SGLang is developer-facing serving infrastructure applicable across general LLM workloads. The workshop covers model deployment, performance tuning, and benchmarking with lm_eval on GSM8K. The workshop assumes familiarity with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM but provides hands-on guidance for SGLang deployment and optimization. The session is an interactive workshop with hands-on deployment and optimization demonstrations. All supporting evidence is directly quoted from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary:
Philip Kiely opens the workshop emphasizing its interactive nature, introducing himself and co-speaker Yineng Zhang, a core SGLang maintainer who previously worked at Meta on click-through rate ranking and inference optimization before joining Baseten. Zhang also contributes to FlashInfer, which SGLang uses as its attention and sampling kernel library, and is a team member at LMISYS. SGLang is positioned as a production-ready, high-performance serving framework comparable to vLLM and TensorRT-LLM, with day-zero support for new models. The project has grown from a December 2023 arXiv paper to nearly 15,000 GitHub stars in 18 months.

The first hands-on exercise deploys a model using truss (Baseten's packaging tool) to bundle SGLang dependencies and commands into a YAML file deployed to L4 GPUs. Philip emphasizes that using SGLang effectively means understanding available flags, configuration options, support matrices, and flag interactions. Yineng then demonstrates CUDA Graph max batch size optimization using Llama 3 8B instruct with FA3 attention backend on L4 GPU. The default CUDA graph max batch size for L4 is 8, capturing batch sizes 1, 2, 4, 8. When benchmarking with lm_eval at 128 concurrent requests, decode batches exceed 8, disabling CUDA graph and yielding ~155 tokens/sec total (~15 per user). Increasing to 32 keeps CUDA graph enabled during decode. Yineng then demonstrates Eagle 3 speculative decoding, explaining that Eagle derives its draft model from multiple layers of the target model rather than using a separate smaller model. Key tuning parameters include number of steps, depth, top-K, and draft verify tokens. SGLang provides a benchmark script to sweep parameter combinations across batch sizes to find optimal settings. Philip emphasizes using representative prompts for benchmarking since speculation is content-dependent.

Yineng concludes the codebase overview by describing the kernel library (attention, normalization, activation implemented in CUDA), the SGLang router (supporting cache-aware routing), and the SGLang runtime (SRT) as the core Python-based inference runtime supporting disaggregated prefill/decode, constrained decoding, function calling, and OpenAI-compatible serving. New model architectures can be added by referencing existing implementations like Llama. The session closes with community involvement guidance: GitHub issues, good first issue labels, a development roadmap, Slack community, and codebase structure overview. Philip invites attendees to a happy hour with OxenAI and advertises Baseten job openings in infrastructure and model performance. During Q&A, Philip explains SGLang's appeal: configurability, well-documented codebase, and ease of contribution allowing users to unblock themselves without waiting for core developers. He notes security is runtime-agnostic and container-based, and that SGLang's open-source nature suits air-gapped or in-house deployments (e.g., for DoD/financial applications). When asked about vLLM, he notes Baseten uses it for broad compatibility, such as with Gemma models at launch.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to LLM serving with SGLang
sections.summary: Philip Kiely introduces the workshop, himself, and co-speaker Yineng Zhang. Outlines the agenda: introducing SGLang, history, deploying first model, performance optimization, and community involvement. Emphasizes the interactive workshop format.

sections.title: What is SGLang?
sections.summary: Defines SGLang as an open-source fast serving framework for LLMs and VLMs, comparable to vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. Highlights performance, production readiness, day-zero model support, strong open-source ethos, and adoption by Baseten, xAI, and other companies.

sections.title: History of SGLang
sections.summary: Covers SGLang's rapid growth from December 2023 arXiv paper to ~15,000 GitHub stars in 18 months. Yineng Zhang introduces himself, his background at Meta, involvement with FlashInfer, and role as core maintainer and LMISYS team member.

sections.title: Deploying Your First Model
sections.summary: Hands-on deployment exercise using truss to package SGLang on Baseten L4 GPUs. Explains that SGLang is essentially a server command with flags, and effective use requires understanding available flags and their interactions. Participants deploy and call models using OpenAI SDK.

sections.title: Optimizing Performance with CUDA Graph Max Batch Size
sections.summary: Yineng demonstrates CUDA Graph max batch size optimization using Llama 3 8B instruct with FA3 attention backend on L4 GPU. Shows that default max batch size of 8 causes CUDA graph to disable when decode batch exceeds 8 concurrent requests (e.g., 10 requests yields ~155 tokens/sec total, ~15 per user). Increasing to 32 keeps CUDA graph enabled during decode. lm_eval used with GSM8K dataset at 128 concurrent requests for benchmarking.

sections.title: Optimizing Performance with Eagle 3 Speculative Decoding
sections.summary: Philip and Yineng demonstrate Eagle 3 speculative decoding configuration. Eagle 3 derives its draft model from multiple layers of the target model rather than using a separate smaller model. Key parameters include speculative decoding algorithm, draft model path, number of steps/depth, top-K, and draft verify tokens. SGLang provides a parameter sweep benchmark script testing combinations across batch sizes. Philip emphasizes using representative production prompts since speculation is content-dependent.

sections.title: SGLang Community and Contributions
sections.summary: Covers community involvement: GitHub issues, good first issue and help wanted labels (~26 open), development roadmap, Slack community at slack.sglang.ai, and Twitter. Codebase overview includes SGLang runtime, domain-specific frontend language, and optimized kernels. Deep Wiki page and community repositories provide codebase tours for new contributors.

sections.title: Codebase Deep Dive: Kernels, Router, and Runtime
sections.summary: Yineng describes the kernel library implementing attention, normalization, and activation in CUDA, welcoming contributions from those interested in kernel programming. Covers the SGLang router with cache-aware routing and the SGLang runtime (SRT) as the core Python inference runtime supporting disaggregated prefill/decode, constrained decoding, function calling, and OpenAI-compatible serving. New model architectures can be added by referencing existing implementations like Llama, since popular open-source models share similar architectures.

sections.title: Invitations and Job Opportunities
sections.summary: Philip wraps up by thanking attendees and issuing two invitations: a happy hour with OxenAI (a fine-tuning company whose CEO fine-tuned Qwen 0.6B to beat GPT 4.1 on a SQL generation benchmark), and job opportunities at Baseten for infrastructure and model performance roles. He notes he will be available at the Baseten booth for all three days of the conference.

sections.title: Q&A
sections.summary: Philip answers audience questions. On why use SGLang: configurability, well-documented codebase, and ease of contribution let users unblock themselves without waiting for core developers. On security: runtime-agnostic, container-based, with least privilege and isolation handled at the platform level. For DoD/financial applications: SGLang's open-source nature enables air-gapped deployments where code can be fully inspected and locked to a release. On vLLM: Baseten uses it for broad compatibility (e.g., Gemma models at launch); TensorRT-LLM is also used heavily. Blockchain/quantum computing integration is not something the speakers have experience with.

demonstrations: Hands-on deployment of first model using SGLang via truss packaging on Baseten L4 GPUs
CUDA Graph max batch size optimization demo using Llama 3 8B instruct model with FA3 attention backend on L4 GPU, comparing default (8) vs. tuned (32)
Benchmarking running SGLang server using lm_eval with GSM8K dataset at 128 concurrent requests
Eagle 3 speculative decoding configuration and parameter tuning demo using a sweep benchmark script
SGLang community and codebase overview on GitHub
limitations: Baseten does not provide SSH access into GPUs for security reasons; lm_eval command shown in demo requires SSH access
Turning on a major speculation algorithm while also jacking up batch size may not work well
Speculative decoding benchmarking on non-representative data will likely yield wrong parameters
Wi-Fi issues during live workshop slowed deployment and caused typos
Speakers had no experience integrating SGLang with blockchain or quantum computing use cases
